planting.note: Set container-grown plants in spring so roots establish before the first winter; this cultivar is a touch less cold-hardy than 'Helleri' and struggles below Zone 6b.

directions: Stokes forms a dense, boxwood-like mound of small glossy leaves on a male plant that never sets berries, making it a tidy choice for low hedges and topiary shapes. Give it well-drained, acidic soil and consistent moisture while it establishes, then expect slow, compact growth that needs only occasional shearing to stay neat. Because it is slightly more cold-sensitive than other dwarf Japanese hollies, site it with some winter wind protection in the colder part of its range.

planting.note: Plant in spring in gritty, well-drained acidic soil; growth is extremely slow, so a nursery-size plant may take many years to fill a rock garden niche.

directions: Piccolo is among the slowest-growing Japanese holly selections, gaining only about an inch a year and forming a tight, dense mound of tiny dark leaves. It is best used in rock gardens, troughs, or as a miniature specimen rather than a hedge, since decades may pass before it reaches knee height. It tolerates light shearing but needs little pruning on its own, and it prefers cooler summers, performing poorly where heat and humidity are both high.

planting.note: Transplant in spring into acidic, well-drained soil; this slow-growing female selection fruits most heavily once a few seasons old.

directions: Berries Jubilee is a mounding Chinese holly grown for its unusually heavy crop of large, bright red berries that cling to the branches well into winter. Give it full sun for the densest fruit set and bluish-green foliage, though it also tolerates part shade with a looser habit. It needs little pruning to maintain its rounded form and, like other Chinese hollies, shrugs off heat, humidity, and short dry spells once established.

planting.note: Transplant in spring into moist, acidic, well-drained soil; a male American holly nearby is needed for this female selection to set its showy fruit.

directions: Clarendon Spreading is an unusual low, ground-hugging sport of American holly that stays only a few feet tall while creeping outward to eight feet or more, in sharp contrast to the species' typical tree form. Glossy olive-green foliage and orange-red fall berries make it a distinctive evergreen groundcover or bank planting for a female pollinator-dependent holly. It accepts full sun to part shade and average garden moisture but, like other American hollies, resents waterlogged soil.

planting.note: Transplant in spring into moist to wet, acidic soil; pair with a male cultivar such as 'Southern Gentleman' for reliable berry set.

directions: Oosterwijk is a Dutch-selected female winterberry prized for its heavy load of bright red fruit on bare branches from fall through winter, and it was historically cut for the European Christmas cut-branch trade. It is deciduous, so the berries show best once the bronze-toned fall foliage drops, and it tolerates wetter, even clay, soils better than most shrubs as long as they stay acidic. A compatible male winterberry planted nearby is required to pollinate the flowers and produce fruit.

planting.note: Transplant in spring into well-drained, acidic soil with some shelter from harsh winter sun and wind, which can scorch variegated foliage.

directions: Honey Maid is a variegated sport of the blue holly group, with blue-green leaves broadly edged in cream and gold that brighten through the seasons, set off by bright red winter berries on this female selection. Its pyramidal habit and slow, dense growth suit it to specimen use or a mixed evergreen screen rather than a tightly clipped hedge. Light afternoon shade helps protect the variegated leaf margins from winter burn, and a male blue holly planted nearby ensures fruit set.
